body:
The three inputs converge on a crucial point: the material does not license a single diagnosis, and each proposed intervention carries assumptions that the stated facts cannot confirm. The account treats the memory-gap as central; the objection reverses that ordering to make avoidance load-bearing; the rival holds multiple readings open and proposes a diagnostic probe before any remedy. I find the rival's restraint most useful here — not because it is correct, but because it resists the slide from plausible reading to established fact that all three inputs warn against.

What I will carry forward from the account is the concrete proposal of a written record and check-in, but repositioned as the rival suggests: not as the remedy following from a diagnosis, but as a test that might discriminate between readings. If disputes drop after recording begins, the memory-gap reading gains weight; if they persist or relocate to the record itself, the normative or standing-negotiation readings gain weight. This treats the intervention as inquiry rather than solution.

From the objection, I take the distinction between memorial and normative disagreement as essential. A written record can settle who said what; it cannot settle what 'done' means when schedules shift, unless that meaning is also recorded at the moment of agreement. This means any record must include scope, recurrence, and timing explicitly — not just task and person. The objection's point that a weekly check-in may ask the group to do more of what already failed is also worth holding: if the avoiding friend does not re-engage after the record is introduced, that outcome should count against the memory-gap reading rather than being explained away.

From the rival, I adopt the probe proposal with modification: before introducing a record, ask each flatmate separately what they thought a past agreement meant, but frame it as the rival suggests — curiosity about their view of the group conversations, not interrogation about their avoidance. This serves two purposes: it gathers data about whether disagreements cluster around scope, recurrence, or timing; and it tests whether one-to-one conversation is possible without reproducing the group dynamic.

What I reject or leave open: I will not treat avoidance as either symptom or cause until the household's own responses discriminate between those readings. I will not assume the written record is an improvement without observing whether disputes relocate rather than resolve. I will not rank mediator, chore reassignment, or formalization as better or worse routes — the material does not support that ranking, and naming them as possibilities is not endorsement.

The path forward is therefore iterative: probe first to see where disagreements cluster; introduce a record with explicit scope if the probe suggests memorial confusion; watch whether disputes drop or relocate; approach the avoiding friend with framing that names curiosity rather than correction; and treat all outcomes as data about which reading fits, not as confirmation of any single diagnosis. This is slower than the account's original proposal, but it honors the objection's and rival's shared caution about diagnostic confidence.
commitments:
Taking this synthesis up involves several distinct commitments, each revisable on its own grounds.

First, a diagnostic commitment: I am treating the three readings (memory-gap, avoidance-as-central, scope/standing-negotiation) as live alternatives rather than settling on one. If someone takes this up, they would be accepting that the diagnosis remains underdetermined until the household's responses to the probe and record provide discriminating data. This is a claim about what the material shows, not about what is happening in the flat.

Second, an intervention commitment: the written record and weekly check-in are proposed as testable interventions, not validated remedies. Their relevance depends on whether disputes drop or relocate after introduction. A quiet week would be uninformative; sustained reduction in 'what was agreed' disputes would support the memory-gap reading; persistent or relocated disputes would support the normative or standing-negotiation readings. This commits to watching for specific outcomes rather than treating any outcome as confirmation.

Third, a probe commitment: asking each flatmate separately about past agreements before introducing a record. This carries the risk that the question itself may be read as interrogation, and that recollection is already in dispute. Taking this up means accepting that the probe may return nothing decisive, and committing to not treating non-clustering answers as evidence for whichever reading one already favored.

Fourth, a framing commitment for the avoidant friend: the one-to-one conversation should be framed as curiosity about their view of group conversations, not as asking why they avoid. This inherits the uncertainty of the readings above — if avoidance is about being unheard in the group, this framing may help; if it is about something else entirely, it may not. The commitment is to the framing, not to its effectiveness.

Fifth, an unresolved problem I am not papering over: I do not know whether the household is willing to formalize anything, whether the avoiding friend will engage in one-to-one conversation, whether the probe will cluster around scope/recurrence/timing or scatter, or whether a record will be read as surveillance. These are genuine gaps. A mediator, different labor division, or naming avoidance as the primary problem could all be better routes, and nothing in the material lets me rank them.

What I am not committing to: I am not claiming the account is wrong, that avoidance is really about status, that the avoidant friend is being outnumbered, or that any particular chore is neglected. Those would be inventions. The commitment is to holding alternatives open long enough for the household's own responses to discriminate between them, and to reporting what actually happens rather than what fits a preferred reading.
